A0050.title: Data Loss Prevention
A0050.definition: Also known as DLP (Data Loss Prevention), a collection of technologies that protect data from leakage through classification, labeling, monitoring, and blocking.
A0050.description: Through content inspection, policy rules, real-time monitoring, and encryption, DLP systems can deeply scan data, identify specific patterns or keywords, monitor real-time data flows to quickly respond to potential leakage risks, and use encryption to protect data security. DLP systems can also implement protections on endpoint devices, monitor network traffic and communication channels, generate detailed reports and audit logs, and enhance employee awareness of sensitive information protection through user education and training.
A0050.limitation: The limitations of DLP systems include false positives, content recognition challenges, endpoint device limitations, uncontrolled endpoint devices, insider threats, real-time latency, complexity, and implementation costs. Organizations must consider and manage these comprehensively during deployment.

references.title: [PDF] Guide to Protecting the Confidentiality of Personally
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations (SC-7, SC-8, SC-28)

A0050-001.title: Data Storage Encryption
A0050-001.definition: Encrypting data to ensure its security on storage media.
A0050-001.description: Data storage encryption can be divided into two types: encrypting data before storing it, or encrypting the storage medium itself. The former allows finer-grained control over data but requires storing the key on the storage medium, so key security must be ensured. The latter does not require storing the key on the storage medium but provides coarser-grained control over data.
A0050-001.limitation: Key management: the security of encryption depends on proper key management. If keys are poorly managed, they may be leaked or lost, making data unrecoverable or accessible to unauthorized parties. Performance impact: the encryption and decryption process may introduce some performance overhead. For large-scale data storage and frequent data access, encryption may cause certain delays.

references.title: Recommendation for Key Management - NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5

A0050-002.title: Database Auditing
A0050-002.definition: Real-time recording and auditing of database access, queries, and changes, relying on audit logs to trace unauthorized access, sensitive data exfiltration, and anomalous changes.
A0050-002.description:
Database auditing captures SQL statements and their results via audit plugins on the database instance, network mirroring, or proxy capture, retaining audit logs along dimensions such as access account, source IP, SQL fingerprint, affected rows, and sensitive-field hits, covering high-risk actions like DBA privileged operations, bulk exports, DDL changes, and sensitive-table queries.

After a data leak or unauthorized access incident, audit logs support reconstructing the operation chain, pinpointing the responsible account and affected data scope, satisfying compliance requirements such as MLPS 2.0, GDPR, and PCI-DSS. Combined with real-time rules, it can alert on anomalous bulk queries, full-table exports, or off-hours DDL, serving as the tracing and forensics layer of the data leakage protection (A0050) system.
A0050-002.limitation: Auditing incurs extra I/O and storage overhead; in high-frequency write scenarios it may be disabled or sampled by ops, causing key operations to go unrecorded. Attackers with DBA privileges can directly disable auditing, tamper with, or clear audit logs to defeat traceability. Operations on encrypted columns and stored procedures are hard to recover in plaintext, and the retention period and retrieval of massive audit logs are constrained by storage cost; excessive false positives tend to be ignored by ops.

references.title: Guide to Computer Security Log Management - NIST SP 800-92

A0050-003.title: Data Erasure
A0050-003.definition: Using multi-pass overwrite, degaussing, or physical destruction to make sensitive data on storage media unrecoverable by software or laboratory methods, securing data on decommissioned devices.
A0050-003.description:
Data erasure targets scenarios such as device decommissioning, resale, repair, or disposal, using specialized tools to perform multi-pass overwrites (e.g., the three passes of DoD 5220.22-M), degaussing, or cryptographic erasure on storage media so that original data cannot be recovered. Unlike ordinary deletion or formatting, which only clears the file-system index while raw data remains on the medium, secure erasure directly destroys the underlying bits so recovery tools cannot restore them.

It is the final step of full-lifecycle data management and is commonly paired with data-at-rest encryption (A0050-001): cryptographic erasure only needs to destroy the key to render ciphertext unreadable, dramatically shortening erasure time for large-capacity media and suited to SSDs that are hard to overwrite block by block. After erasure, an auditable erasure report is typically generated, recording the device serial number, erasure algorithm, time, and operator as compliance evidence.
A0050-003.limitation: Multi-pass overwrite is time-consuming on large mechanical drives and wears the medium. Solid-state drives cannot guarantee physical erasure of every block via logical overwrite due to wear leveling and over-provisioning, and must rely on vendor ATA Secure Erase or physical shredding to be reliable. Cryptographic erasure depends on secure key destruction; if a key backup exists or leaks, data remains recoverable. The erasure process is irreversible, and misoperation causes permanent business data loss; residual data has been recovered from retired devices that had already entered the second-hand market.

references.title: Guidelines for Media Sanitization - NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 1
